questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: ETH's overall academic reputation. I also insisted on high-functioning infrastructure.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was majorly surprised by how many social activities and friends i made along the way. I was dissapointed by ETH, though, as the quality of the actuarial courses was lacking.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. There was multiple dates where one could ask questions.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of paperwork and regulatory stuff. One should keep a good notebook to keep a birds eye view.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There were many mails and information about various mandatory things scatterd around the place. It would have been nice if it was more centralized.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
I entered a housing lottery, and was lucky enough to get it. My gut-feeling tells me it was around 90% that got it.
It was, however, an unpleasant experience, since i wasn't sure if I was getting scammed. It would be nice with actual 2-factor authentication or a login to a website etc. This was just an email, that told me to wire 35000kr (for the whole stay).
The allocation of rooms also took place late (around 15. juli), so i would have had to find a room quickly.
When the dust settled, however, I was very happy with my living situation.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Usually, one either has a good social life, but poor living conditions (like 170 people sharing one industry kitchen), or good facilities, but poor social life. I was whole-heartedly blessed when i got my room, even though it was shared bathrooms and only one big kitchen. The social life spawning from 170 exchange students in the exact same predicatment made more than up for it. 
Spontanious-hikes, skiing-days, poker-nights and the odd ping-pong match in the evening was, surprisingly (for me), what made the exchange worth it, even though i initially thought it was going to be the academic opportunities that would make it worth.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very easy. One can still sign up/drop courses the first two weeks they are taught. Thus, one can try out multiple courses before commiting. However, one should come prepared with pre-approval for potential candidate courses, as one does not have the time to get approval before having to commit otherwise. One should also pay lots of attention to the ECTS and time-slot situation, since the odd course sizing makes it more difficult compared to the simple 7,5 ECTS with 3 schedule groups at home.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: One just adds courses in the MyStudies portal from a list

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Peers would definently have figured it out, even if you didn't. It's very easy, so i never looked for help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Yes, I was. I should have tried out more courses though, as many of them (3/5) dissapointed

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Previous comments.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Their actuarial courses are of much lower quality, since their actuarial education is shorter than ours. Their mathematical finance courses, however, were much more theoretical and hard. One also either incur large overlap with previously taken courses (which i recommend) or lack prerequisites (which is hard, especially at ETH). The further you are with your education, the more this applies.
Also, the credits are very expensive (meaning that 30 credits feels like much more)
I suggest picking courses in a way such that exams are of different kinds, to ease the burden of exams. My 5 oral exams was a bad idea.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was kinda hard to understand what was what, since it appears in different levels on different study programs. I filtered by MA, but i ended up with some courses that were also meant for BA.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
I found it much less pedagogical, and (in actuarial courses) worse. This is most likely because some of these courses were taught by practitioners, so their theoretical capabilities was notably lacking (atleast I thought so, even if my class mates didnt).
The courses taught by professors, however, were very hard and expected a lot from the student in terms of academic maturity. (Good study ethic, etc.)
My peers (in different fields, engineering) were very impressed though.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Mathematical finance 10 ECTS - Dylan Possamai
Non-life insurance 8 ECTS - Mario wüthrich
Mathematical models in life insurance 4 ECTS - Tobias Jonas Peter
Smoothing and non-parametric regression 4 ECTS - Sucarita Beran-Ghosh
Financial risk management in social and pension insurance 4 ECTS - Peter Blum

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Mathematical finance: Brutally hard course. If you are not very theoretically interested, avoid it. Poorly taught, bad structure in the course, but extremely good for you, if you put in the work. I spent 50-60% of my total study time on just this one. Very much depends on the lecturer, so if it is not dylan, it will probably be very different. 
Non-life insurance (20-30% of my time): Very good balance of application and theory. Every non-life acturary should know this. It is less theoretical than courses at home, but more theoretical than the application based courses. It hits the perfect sweet-spot. Alot of overlap with Skade1 though.
Mathematical models in life insurance (5-10% of my time): Horrible course. There is little-to-no-math going on here. 
Smoothing and non-parametric regression  (5-10% of my time): Pretty easy course, which was poorly taught. Big overlap with Statins from UCPH
Financial risk management in social and pension insurance (5-10% of my time): Poorly taught course, with many glaring holes from the models being too simple.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I didn't expect to go skiing, but the people i meet convinced me :)
Various random things cost money, such as going to the immigrations office, (which is mandatory). 
I also had to go to the dentist which could have been very expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and especially take-away was more expensive than anticipated. If you avoid Coop and go to lidl it is ok.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The sports programme is very easy to join, and every week (24 hours before the class) you have to sign up. This makes it extremely easy to try new things. I tried the following
Table Tennis 10 times
Ultimate freesbee 1 time
Boxing 1 time
Bouldering 1 time
Basketball 2 times
I wish i had tried more things.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Mostly sports. Loads of them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Previously mentioned sport activities. 
Polyball was supposedly very nice too.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Hike/ski with your fellow exchange student friends.
Make a cake, bathe in the river. All the things you do with friends.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go for it. I wish i had indulged more in such relations.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I barely interacted with them.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
They are strict about times, so trains come on time.
They are also very friendly and harmless. Hundreds of people in the libraries just leave computer and everything for multiple hours when they go to lunch break. As far as i know, nothing was stolen. Culture is very trust-based like that

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: You should like to study, and have high study-maturity. You have to put in significant work, on your own terms.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just try courses before comitting. One can interact with the same material on very different levels, and it can be hard to gauge from a description. 3 of my 5 courses were too easy, and 1 was too hard/intenstive.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Growing as a person from new expiriences - good and bad.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Mathematical finance - by far. (and i aced the 15 ECTS master course at home beforehand, plus some more finance courses)

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
